title: Attention with Routed-Memory for Learnable Sparse Control
claim: Our method occupies an unexplored corner among caching paradigms, using a routed, gated memory update to achieve bounded growth without information loss.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, zoom-in from taxonomy triangle to detailed module diagram
description: Three panels read left to right, linked by thick black arrows that zoom in on the method. Left: a triangle diagram of caching paradigms. Its corners are Cache Offloading, Cache Eviction and Cache Quantization, in purple ovals. Its edges are labeled Bounded Memory Growth, Full Prior Token Information and No CPU-GPU Memory Transfer. A red 'Ours' oval sits at the center. Middle: a teal-framed 'Cache Updating' box. A token enters a binary-tree hierarchical cache (yellow, with Bucket Selection). Below it a pink Memory Updating region has a dashed Gate/Memory Mixing box, a Cache Update loop and an Updated Memory node. Right: a detailed flowchart. The incoming token goes to a Gumbel-Softmax routing policy, which selects among slots 1..N holding K/V pairs. A sigmoid gate with α and 1-α combines the new key-value with the stored one, and a purple feedback arrow returns the updated bucket. Orange, yellow, pink and purple dominate.
caption: Outline of our ARM caching structure and the space it falls within the different caching paradigms. For any incoming token, memory slots are selected from the hierarchical cache using a memory controller. The selected slots are used for attention computation. At the same time, the memory slot is updated through a gated memory update.
abstract: Despite advances in long-context inference, large language models (LLMs) remain fundamentally limited by the key-value (KV) caching mechanisms that are necessary for stable computation. Techniques such as selective token eviction and pruning have vastly mitigated these issues, but often discard core information to manage the growing cache. In this paper, we propose Attention with Routed Memory (ARM) a novel KV caching structure that introduces a fully differentiable, fixed-size memory system organized as a hierarchical router. Via a Gumbel-Softmax, ARM learns to select memory slots and perform sigmoid-gated updates that softly combine new and stored information, avoiding hard eviction and reducing information loss. By further training a policy to dynamically select varying amounts of memory at inference, ARM adapts its accesses for both simple contexts and inputs that require deeper reasoning, enabling more scalable and effective retrieval on both short- and long-contexts. Experimental results on standard commonsense and long-context reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ARM achieves superior performance and efficiency compared to fixed KV-caching approaches, while remaining efficient and scalable in terms of both memory and generation latency.
